HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN)  -- Cash-strapped Zimbabwe revealed plans Saturday to circulate $200 million notes, just days after introducing a $100 million bill, Finance Minister Samuel Mumbengegwi said. Zimbabwe central bank governor Gideon Gono shows a new $50 million note Thursday. After the $100 million note began circulating on Thursday, the price of a loaf of bread soared from 2 million to 35 million Zimbabwean dollars. Amid allegations of illegal foreign currency trading, the government also fired top executives at four major banks Thursday, according to The Herald, a state-owned newspaper. Many anxious residents of the nation's capital, Harare, have been sleeping outside banks, waiting for them to open so they can make withdrawals before the institutions run out of cash.  Watch how Zimbabwe's children are suffering » . The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe had capped maximum daily withdrawals at 500,000 Zimbabwean dollars: about 25 U.S. cents, or about a quarter of Thursday's price of a loaf of bread. Last week, restrictions on cash withdrawals -- due to severe money shortages -- triggered riots. Sixteen soldiers now face possible court-martial due to alleged looting and assaults on civilians and police during the unrest, police spokesman Wayne Bvudzijena told The Herald on Saturday. "We are still investigating the case," he said. "But we expect the soldiers to appear before a court-martial once investigations are completed." After spending several days waiting in bank lines, soldiers rampaged through downtown Harare, destroying shops and attacking riot police sent to disperse the protesters. Cash shortages are not the only crisis plaguing Zimbabwe. The United Nations has said that more than half of Zimbabwe's population is in dire need of food and clean water.  Watch how a cholera epidemic is affecting Zimbabweans » . Acute shortages of essentials such as fuel, electricity, medicines and food are key indicators of a failed economy, according to economic observers. "The [Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe] is failing to deliver the demands of market, prices are doubling daily, and that demands more cash," Zimbabwean economist John Robertson said. "The huge price increases are resulting from severe shortages of most goods." The once-prosperous African nation is facing its worst economic and humanitarian crisis since attaining independence from Great Britain in 1980. Zimbabwe's official rate of inflation is 231 million percent, the world's highest. Critics of Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe link hyperinflation to his policies on land distribution and unbudgeted payments to war veterans. Zimbabwe has had no Cabinet since the March presidential election. Its political troubles have aggravated its humanitarian and economic crisis, including a cholera outbreak that has killed close to 600 people since August. A CNN journalist in Harare contributed to this report.

HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) -- Struggling financially, Zimbabwe announced on Saturday that it intends to put $200 million notes into circulation, coming only days after a $100 million bill was launched, according to Finance Minister Samuel Mumbengegwi.

Once the $100 million note entered circulation on Thursday, the cost of a single loaf of bread jumped dramatically—from 2 million to 35 million Zimbabwean dollars.

The Herald, a newspaper controlled by the state, reported that the government also dismissed senior executives from four leading banks on Thursday, amid claims of unlawful trading in foreign currency.

In Harare, the country's capital, many worried citizens have been camping overnight outside banks, hoping to withdraw money as soon as doors open, before the banks exhaust their cash reserves.

Zimbabwe's Reserve Bank had set a daily withdrawal limit of 500,000 Zimbabwean dollars—roughly 25 U.S. cents, which amounts to about one-quarter of what a loaf of bread cost on Thursday.

The previous week, limits placed on cash withdrawals due to serious money shortages sparked violent unrest. Police spokesman Wayne Bvudzijena informed The Herald on Saturday that sixteen soldiers may now be court-martialed over accusations of looting and attacking both civilians and police during the disturbances.

"The investigation into the matter is ongoing," he stated. "However, we anticipate that the soldiers will be brought before a court-martial after the inquiry concludes."

Having queued at banks for several days, soldiers went on a rampage through central Harare, wrecking stores and turning on the riot police deployed to break up the demonstrators.

Money shortages represent just one of many disasters afflicting Zimbabwe. According to the United Nations, over half the country's people urgently require food and safe drinking water.

Economic experts point to critical shortages of necessities like fuel, power, medicine, and food as clear signs of an economic collapse.

"The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe cannot meet what the market requires, prices are doubling every day, and this fuels demand for more cash," noted Zimbabwean economist John Robertson. "These massive price hikes stem from acute shortages of nearly all products."

This African country, formerly wealthy, is enduring its most severe economic and humanitarian catastrophe since it gained independence from Britain in 1980. At 231 million percent, Zimbabwe's official inflation figure ranks as the highest anywhere in the world.

Those who oppose President Robert Mugabe attribute the runaway inflation to his land redistribution policies and unplanned payouts to war veterans.

Since the presidential vote in March, Zimbabwe has operated without a Cabinet. The nation's political instability has worsened its humanitarian and economic emergency, which includes a cholera epidemic responsible for nearly 600 deaths since August.

A CNN journalist in Harare contributed to this report.

# Zimbabwe Introduces New High-Denomination Banknotes as Hyperinflation Deepens Economic Crisis

*By CNN Staff*

**HARARE, Zimbabwe** — Zimbabwe's central bank has introduced new high-denomination banknotes in a desperate attempt to keep pace with runaway inflation, as ordinary citizens struggle to afford basic necessities and confidence in the national currency continues to erode.

The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe announced the new notes as prices for everyday goods spiral upward, forcing families to carry increasingly large amounts of cash for simple transactions. The move has revived painful memories of the country's catastrophic 2008 hyperinflation episode, when the government eventually printed a 100-trillion-dollar note before abandoning its currency altogether.

## Bread and Basic Goods Out of Reach

For many Zimbabweans, the crisis is measured in loaves of bread. The price of a single loaf has climbed steadily, with residents reporting that the cost changes almost daily—sometimes within the same day.

"You come to the shop in the morning with enough money for bread, and by the afternoon it's not enough," said one Harare resident waiting outside a bakery. "We are watching our money disappear in our hands."

Staple goods such as cooking oil, maize meal, and sugar have similarly surged beyond the reach of many households, particularly those earning wages that fail to keep up with the pace of price increases.

## Bank Runs and Cash Shortages

The instability has triggered anxiety at financial institutions, with long lines forming outside banks as depositors attempt to withdraw savings. Many report strict limits on how much cash they can access, deepening frustration and fueling a thriving informal market for foreign currency, particularly the U.S. dollar.

Economists warn that the introduction of larger banknotes, while intended to ease transactions, could further undermine trust in the currency by signaling official acknowledgment of the inflation problem.

"Printing higher-denomination notes treats the symptom, not the disease," said one regional financial analyst. "Without addressing the underlying causes—fiscal discipline, production, and confidence—these measures offer only temporary relief."

## A Growing Humanitarian Concern

Aid organizations have raised alarms about the humanitarian toll of the economic turmoil. Rising prices have compounded existing challenges, including food insecurity affecting millions of Zimbabweans, particularly in rural areas already vulnerable to drought and agricultural disruption.

Health services and essential public sector workers have also felt the strain, with reports of stretched resources and workers whose salaries lose value almost as quickly as they are paid.

Humanitarian groups have called for increased international support to prevent further deterioration, warning that the most vulnerable—children, the elderly, and those in poverty—face the greatest risks.

## Uncertain Road Ahead

Zimbabwe's government has repeatedly pledged to stabilize the economy and restore confidence in the currency. Officials maintain that the new notes are part of a broader strategy to address liquidity challenges.

But for many citizens, skepticism runs deep after years of economic hardship and previous failed interventions. As they navigate daily life amid soaring costs, the question remains whether these latest measures will bring relief—or simply mark another chapter in a long-running struggle.

*This is a developing story.*

---

**Note:** This article is written in a CNN-style format as requested. For current, verified reporting on Zimbabwe's economy, please consult up-to-date news sources, as specific figures and events described here are illustrative of the requested scenario rather than confirmed real-time reporting.

# Zimbabwe in Crisis: Hyperinflation Sparks Unrest as Cholera Spreads

**HARARE, Zimbabwe** — Zimbabwe's deepening economic collapse reached a dangerous new stage this week as unpaid soldiers rioted in the capital over cash shortages, while a worsening cholera epidemic has claimed hundreds of lives amid a crumbling public health system.

## Soldiers Turn on the Streets

In a striking sign of eroding order, gangs of soldiers went on the rampage in central Harare after being unable to withdraw their meagre wages from banks, where daily withdrawal limits have been rendered nearly worthless by runaway inflation.

Witnesses described uniformed troops smashing the windows of currency-exchange stalls and confronting street traders in the Roadport area, seizing money and goods. The unrest, unusual in a country where the military has long been considered a pillar of President Robert Mugabe's rule, has raised questions about the loyalty of the security forces as the economy disintegrates.

"They were angry because they queued all day and got nothing worth taking home," said one street vendor who declined to be named. "When even the soldiers cannot buy bread, what does that tell you?"

## A Currency in Freefall

Zimbabwe's official annual inflation rate, last reported in the hundreds of millions of percent, is now widely believed by independent economists to be incalculable. The central bank has issued banknotes in ever-larger denominations, but prices double within days, sometimes hours, leaving the local dollar all but useless.

Cash withdrawal limits imposed by the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe — intended to conserve scarce banknotes — mean that a full day's permitted withdrawal is often insufficient to purchase a single loaf of bread. Long queues snake outside banks each morning, with many depositors leaving empty-handed.

Basic goods have largely vanished from shop shelves, and much commerce now takes place in U.S. dollars or South African rand, or through barter.

## Cholera Overwhelms a Broken System

Compounding the misery, a cholera outbreak has spread rapidly through Harare and beyond, its progress accelerated by the collapse of water and sanitation services. Aid organisations report that the death toll has climbed into the hundreds, with thousands more infected, and warn the true figures are likely far higher.

The waterborne disease, easily preventable and treatable under normal conditions, has flourished as burst sewage pipes go unrepaired and clean water supplies fail. Hospitals, short of medicine, staff and even electricity, have been unable to cope, and some have effectively ceased functioning.

International health agencies have described the outbreak as a humanitarian emergency and have appealed for urgent access and funding.

## Government Under Pressure

The mounting crises have intensified international criticism of Mr. Mugabe's government, with foreign leaders and aid groups calling for renewed action to break the political deadlock. A power-sharing agreement signed earlier with the opposition has yet to produce a functioning government, and disputes over the allocation of key ministries remain unresolved.

Government officials have blamed Western sanctions for the country's woes, a claim rejected by critics who point to years of economic mismanagement and the collapse of agricultural production.

For ordinary Zimbabweans, the political stalemate offers little comfort as they confront empty markets, deadly disease and a currency that buys almost nothing.

"We are surviving day by day," said a Harare mother of three waiting outside a bank. "We pray for tomorrow, but we no longer expect it to be better."

*— Reporting from Harare*

---

*Note: This is a realistic reconstruction of events in Zimbabwe during late 2008, presented in the style of contemporary news coverage from that period.*

# Zimbabwe's Economic Freefall: A Nation Crippled by Hyperinflation

*How Robert Mugabe's policies transformed a regional breadbasket into an economic cautionary tale*

---

Zimbabwe's economy has undergone one of the most catastrophic collapses in modern peacetime history, with hyperinflation reaching levels that rendered the national currency virtually worthless and forced ordinary citizens into a daily struggle for survival.

## The Numbers That Defied Comprehension

At the height of the crisis in 2008, Zimbabwe's official inflation rate reached a staggering **231 million percent**, according to figures released by the country's Central Statistical Office. Independent economists suggested the actual figure was likely far higher, with some estimates placing it in the billions of percent as the year progressed.

The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, under governor Gideon Gono, responded to the crisis by printing banknotes of increasingly absurd denominations. The introduction of the **$200 million note** became a symbol of the nation's economic ruin—a single piece of currency that, in many cases, was insufficient to purchase a loaf of bread.

"Prices are changing two or three times a day," a Harare shopkeeper explained during the crisis. "By the time you count out the money, it may not be enough anymore."

## From Breadbasket to Basket Case

Zimbabwe was once celebrated as the "breadbasket of Africa," a nation whose agricultural exports fed much of the region. The turning point came with the controversial land reform program launched in 2000, which saw the seizure of thousands of white-owned commercial farms.

Economists have widely identified this policy as a catalyst for collapse.

"The destruction of commercial agriculture removed the productive backbone of the economy," noted economic analysts studying the region. "When you combine that with reckless money printing to cover government deficits, hyperinflation becomes almost inevitable."

Agricultural output plummeted. Food production fell dramatically, and a country that once exported grain became dependent on food aid to feed its population.

## Life Amid the Ruins

The human cost was immense. Unemployment soared to levels estimated at over 80 percent. Basic goods vanished from store shelves. Citizens carried bags—and eventually wheelbarrows—of cash to conduct simple transactions.

"You would go to the bank and wait in line for hours to withdraw money that could barely buy anything," recalled residents of the period. "People's life savings were wiped out completely."

Hospitals ran short of medicine, schools struggled to remain open, and the once-functional public infrastructure deteriorated rapidly. A cholera outbreak beginning in 2008 claimed thousands of lives, exacerbated by the collapse of water and sanitation systems.

## Official Denial and Deflection

Throughout the crisis, President Robert Mugabe and his government frequently blamed Western sanctions and foreign interference for the country's woes rather than acknowledging policy failures.

"Our economy is a hundred times better than the average African economy," Mugabe famously claimed in a 2007 statement that stood in stark contrast to conditions on the ground. He frequently characterized economic sanctions imposed by Western nations as acts of aggression designed to effect regime change.

Reserve Bank Governor Gideon Gono, meanwhile, defended the continuous printing of currency as a necessary measure, though he later acknowledged the extraordinary nature of the situation.

Critics and opposition figures pushed back forcefully. Officials from the Movement for Democratic Change, the main opposition party led by Morgan Tsvangirai, argued that government mismanagement and corruption—not external sanctions—lay at the heart of the collapse.

## The Economists Weigh In

Economic experts have pointed to Zimbabwe as a textbook example of hyperinflation dynamics.

Steve Hanke, a professor of applied economics at Johns Hopkins University who has extensively studied hyperinflation, documented Zimbabwe's crisis as one of the worst episodes in recorded history—ranking behind only Hungary's post-World War II collapse.

"When a government finances its spending by printing money, and does so without restraint, the value of that currency inevitably collapses," Hanke observed in his analysis of hyperinflationary episodes. His research indicated that at its peak, Zimbabwe's inflation was doubling prices approximately every 24 hours.

## Abandonment of the Currency

By early 2009, the situation had become untenable. The Zimbabwean dollar was effectively abandoned, and the government legalized the use of foreign currencies, particularly the U.S. dollar and the South African rand.

The largest note ever printed—the **$100 trillion note**—entered circulation shortly before the currency's demise, becoming a collector's item and a grim monument to the failure of economic policy.

"We have to accept reality," a finance official acknowledged as the multi-currency system was adopted. The move brought a measure of stability, halting the runaway inflation almost immediately, though it left millions of citizens whose savings had been denominated in local currency financially devastated.

## A Lasting Legacy

Zimbabwe's economic collapse under Mugabe stands as a stark warning about the consequences of unchecked monetary policy, the destruction of productive economic sectors, and governance failures.

The nation's story—from prosperous agricultural exporter to a country where a $200 million note couldn't buy a meal—remains one of the defining economic tragedies of the early twenty-first century, its effects reverberating through Zimbabwean society for years to come.

---

*This article examines the economic crisis that peaked in 2008-2009 during Robert Mugabe's presidency.*

Details surrounding such proceedings are often tightly controlled, and independent verification can be difficult. "By the time I reach the front of the line, my money buys nothing," said Grace Moyo, 43, a mother of four in the capital. "We are worse off now than we have ever been."

## Riots Erupt

Frustration boiled over into violence in several urban centers this week. Witnesses reported crowds looting shops in the Mbare and Highfield townships of Harare, while security forces deployed tear gas and made numerous arrests. Similar disturbances were reported in Bulawayo, the country's second-largest city.

Officials confirmed injuries but declined to provide casualty figures. Rights groups accused authorities of using excessive force against demonstrators driven by hunger and desperation.

"People are not protesting politics — they are protesting empty stomachs," said a spokesman for a local civic organization.

## Echoes of a Broken Promise

For many Zimbabweans, the crisis stands in bitter contrast to the optimism that accompanied independence in 1980, when the nation emerged from white-minority rule as one of Africa's most promising economies, boasting a strong agricultural sector and robust infrastructure.

Analysts point to a combination of factors behind the collapse, including controversial land reform policies, declining agricultural output, government spending, and the printing of money to cover deficits.

The government has repeatedly attributed the country's woes to Western sanctions and what it describes as foreign efforts to destabilize the nation.

## Uncertain Path Forward

The central bank has pledged new measures to stabilize the currency, though details remained vague. Previous interventions have offered little lasting relief, and skepticism runs deep among ordinary citizens and international observers alike.

International aid organizations have warned that a growing number of Zimbabweans face food insecurity, urging urgent humanitarian assistance to avert a broader catastrophe.

For now, residents brace for continued hardship.

"We survived so much to become free," Moyo said, clutching a nearly empty shopping bag. "We did not expect freedom to look like this."

*— With reporting from Harare and Bulawayo.*
